What Makes a Case Study Believable

By lowob · 21 August 2026 · Updated 9 November 2026 · 5-minute read · Revenue / Research

A prospective customer reads your case study because they want to know one thing: have you solved a problem like mine, and can you show me what happened? A client logo, a polished testimonial and a large percentage won't answer that question on their own.

A good case study is closer to a clear account of a project than to an advertisement. It shows the starting situation, the decisions made, what changed, and what the evidence can actually support.

Start with a situation the reader recognizes

“We helped a fintech company grow” tells a potential client almost nothing. What kind of fintech company? Was it struggling to acquire users, get partners to respond or explain a complex product? What could the team afford to try? Which constraints made the job difficult?

For example, an anonymous payments startup with a two-person sales team and a limited marketing budget is already more useful context than “a leading fintech innovator.” The reader can judge whether the example resembles their own business.

Then explain what the provider actually did. Don't say it “optimized the growth engine.” Say that it rewrote an unclear landing page, interviewed five customers, launched a partner referral campaign or stopped spending on ads that brought the wrong people. The specific work is the useful part of the story.

A percentage needs a starting point and a date

Imagine a case study that says “qualified leads increased 40%.” It sounds impressive. But did the company go from five to seven leads a month, or 500 to 700? Was this measured over a week or a year? Did the sales team also hire more people or change the definition of a qualified lead?

Hard to evaluate

“We boosted qualified leads by 40% through our proprietary approach.”

Much more useful

“In this illustrative eight-week project, monthly qualified demo requests rose from 10 to 14 after changes to the website and partner outreach. The team also changed its sales process, so the result cannot be attributed to one activity alone.”

Both statements above are illustrative, not real campaign results. The second tells a reader what the number means and what remains uncertain. That is more valuable than an enormous percentage with no baseline.

Be just as clear about the cost of the work. If the result required six months of engineering, a new salesperson and an expensive advertising budget, that matters to a buyer deciding whether the approach is realistic for them.

The setbacks are part of the evidence

Real projects involve delays, wrong assumptions and changes in direction. Perhaps the first set of ads attracted too many irrelevant visitors. Maybe the original message confused customers. Or a potential partner declined to participate, forcing a different approach.

Leaving out every setback makes a case study harder to believe and less useful. Include one or two meaningful decisions the team changed because of what it learned. That lets the reader see judgment in action rather than a flawless sequence written after the fact.

A direct customer comment can help, especially when it describes what was difficult or surprising. But a quote is not proof of every claimed outcome. The US Federal Trade Commission's guidance on testimonials distinguishes honest endorsements from substantiation of advertising claims. A happy customer can describe their experience; factual performance claims still need support.

When the client can't be named

For regulated financial products, enterprise infrastructure and competitive projects, naming the client or sharing exact figures may not be allowed. That doesn't mean the case study must become useless. It does mean the provider needs explicit permission for whatever it publishes.

Describe the business problem, type of customer, work and outcome at a level the client approves. Use ranges or percentages only when the underlying figures are real and the client agrees to that presentation. Be careful: revealing the geography, company size, product category and timeline together may identify a customer even without its name.

Ask for approval of the project description, individual quotes, performance claims and any screenshots. A composite story based on several engagements may be useful as an industry observation, but it must not be passed off as a single verified customer result.

What if you don't have a case study yet?

Don't manufacture one. Instead, show how you would approach a problem: the questions you'd ask, what you would inspect, the work you'd try first, and what evidence you'd need before recommending more spending.

Then make case-study permission part of the next customer engagement. Agree early on which measurements can be retained and whether the customer might approve a public or anonymous summary. You can't force an endorsement, but you can make it easier to document real work without scrambling for data months later.

One believable story about a modest result is more useful than five vaguely impressive success stories. A prospective customer should leave knowing what happened, what it cost, what might work elsewhere and what still needs to be tested.

lowob takeaways

  • Show the starting situation. A buyer needs to recognize the problem, the customer and the constraints.
  • Describe the actual work. Explain the decisions and changes, including anything that didn't work.
  • Make results checkable. Include a baseline, time period, measurement method and meaningful limitations.
  • Protect customer permission without inventing proof. An anonymous real case can be credible; a hypothetical example must be labeled as such.

Sources and examples

US FTC: Advertising FAQs for Small Business. Referenced for the distinction between endorsements and evidence supporting factual claims.

US FTC: Advertisement Endorsements. Referenced for truthfulness, material connections and avoiding misleading claims.

The lead-growth example is entirely fictional and is included to explain what credible reporting looks like. It is not a lowob client case study.
